## Main Result: "Asking to Clarify: Bridging Ambiguity in Tool-Agent-User Interactions"

The paper presents an evaluation framework built on τ-Bench, in which a dedicated Clarifier module is triggered after tool calls to decide whether and how to ask follow-up questions. The Clarifier is designed to be plug-and-play, operating independently of the agent's internal policy and can be paired with different agent backbones without retraining the agent itself.

To equip this module with strategic questioning capabilities, the authors investigate supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and a user-goal-driven group-wise preference optimization (GRPO) method.

Experiments across domains and agent backbones show that learned clarification consistently improves task success, with user-goal driven GRPO achieving among the strongest cross-domain generalization results.

The paper appears to be available at: https://openreview.net/pdf/1fef23a87110c575bdcaaf67004fcf6606d2af14.pdf

## LHAW: Controllable Underspecification for Long-Horizon Tasks

The paper introduces LHAW (Long-Horizon Augmented Workflows), a modular, dataset-agnostic synthetic pipeline that transforms any well-specified task into controllable underspecified variants by systematically removing information across four dimensions – Goals, Constraints, Inputs, and Context – at configurable severity levels.

### The Taxonomy

The paper defines a structured taxonomy of information dimensions that can be systematically removed from task specifications, which was constructed by analyzing failure modes across 33 TAC tasks and identifying recurring patterns of missing information. The taxonomy was developed by observing what types of information, when absent, caused agents to fail or diverge.

### Key Features

Unlike approaches that rely on LLM predictions of ambiguity, LHAW validates variants through empirical agent trials, classifying them as outcome-critical, divergent, or benign based on observed terminal state divergence.

The authors released 285 task variants from TheAgentCompany, SWE-Bench Pro and MCP-Atlas according to their taxonomy alongside formal analysis measuring how current agents detect, reason about, and resolve underspecification across ambiguous settings.

## Overview

The query "Asking to Clarify: Bridging Ambiguity in Tool-Agent-User Interactions" appears to be a research topic with multiple related papers studying how AI agents handle ambiguous user requests in interactive settings.

## Key Research Areas

One approach extends the standard τ-bench setup by introducing a Clarifier that triggers after tool calls when the agent has not clarified yet may still lack information for a valid next action, yielding a three-part prompting architecture: (1) Domain-Policy Tool Calling governing policy-compliant tool use; (2) User-Driven Fuzzy Intent modeling partially specified user goals; and (3) ReAsk Decision & Generation implementing uncertainty detection and targeted question generation.

## Research Frameworks

Several papers address different aspects of clarification in agent-user interactions:

- A task-agnostic framework for resolving ambiguity by asking users clarifying questions breaks down this objective into three subtasks: (1) determining when clarification is needed, (2) determining what clarifying question to ask, and (3) responding accurately with the new information gathered through clarification.

- A structured uncertainty approach operates directly over tool parameters and their domains, cleanly separating specification uncertainty from model uncertainty, using Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI) to quantify the disambiguation value of each potential question.

- Making unwarranted assumptions to compensate for missing information and failing to ask clarifying questions can lead to suboptimal outcomes, safety risks due to tool misuse, and wasted computational resources, which has prompted research evaluating models on detecting underspecificity, asking targeted clarification questions, and leveraging the interaction to improve performance.

## Paper Summary

arXiv paper 2604.02869 is titled "Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning for Tool-Calling Agents with Iterative Reward Calibration", published on April 3, 2026.

### Key Contributions

The paper presents the first application of MT-GRPO (Multi-Turn Group Relative Policy Optimization) combined with GTPO (Generalized Token-level Policy Optimization) for training a tool-calling agent on realistic customer service tasks with an LLM-based user simulator.

### Main Problem and Solution

Through systematic analysis of training rollouts, the authors discover that naïvely designed dense per-turn rewards degrade performance by up to 14 percentage points due to misalignment between reward discriminativeness and advantage direction.

To address this, they introduce Iterative Reward Calibration (IRC), a methodology for designing per-turn rewards using empirical discriminative analysis of rollout data, and show that their GTPO hybrid advantage formulation eliminates the advantage misalignment problem.

### Results on Tau-Bench

Applied to the Tau-Bench airline benchmark, their approach improves Qwen3.5-4B from 63.8% to 66.7% (+2.9pp) and Qwen3-30B-A3B from 58.0% to 69.5% (+11.5pp), with impressive performance gains on this realistic customer service benchmark.

## LHAW: Controllable Underspecification for Long-Horizon Tasks

LHAW (Long-Horizon Augmented Workflows) is a modular, dataset-agnostic synthetic pipeline that transforms any well-specified task into controllable underspecified variants by systematically removing information across four dimensions - Goals, Constraints, Inputs, and Context - at configurable severity levels.

### Problem It Addresses

Long-horizon workflow agents that operate effectively over extended periods are essential for truly autonomous systems. Their reliable execution critically depends on the ability to reason through ambiguous situations in which clarification seeking is necessary to ensure correct task execution. However, progress is limited by the lack of scalable, task-agnostic frameworks for systematically curating and measuring the impact of ambiguity across custom workflows.

### Methodology

LHAW transforms well-specified benchmark tasks into controllably underspecified variants through three phases: (1) Segment Extraction—identifying removable information segments categorized by dimension (Goal, Constraint, Input, Context) and scored for criticality; (2) Candidate Generation—producing underspecified variants at configurable severity levels; and (3) Empirical Agent Trials—classifying each variant as outcome-critical, divergent, or benign based on observed agent behavior.

### Key Features

Unlike approaches that rely on LLM predictions of ambiguity, LHAW validates variants through empirical agent trials, classifying them as outcome-critical, divergent, or benign based on observed terminal state divergence.

### Dataset Release

The authors release 285 task variants from TheAgentCompany, SWE-Bench Pro and MCP-Atlas according to their taxonomy alongside formal analysis measuring how current agents detect, reason about, and resolve underspecification across ambiguous settings.

## Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning for Tool-Calling Agents with Iterative Reward Calibration

The paper was submitted on April 3, 2026, and authored by Wachiravit Modecrua, Krittanon Kaewtawee, Krittin Pachtrachai, and Touchapon Kraisingkorn from the Amity Research and Application Center (ARAC).

**Main Challenge and Contribution:**

Training tool-calling agents with reinforcement learning on multi-turn tasks remains challenging due to sparse outcome rewards and difficult credit assignment across conversation turns. The paper presents the first application of MT-GRPO (Multi-Turn Group Relative Policy Optimization) combined with GTPO (Generalized Token-level Policy Optimization) for training a tool-calling agent on realistic customer service tasks with an LLM-based user simulator.

**Key Findings:**

Through systematic analysis of training rollouts, they discover that naively designed dense per-turn rewards degrade performance by up to 14 percentage points due to misalignment between reward discriminativeness and advantage direction. They introduce Iterative Reward Calibration, a methodology for designing per-turn rewards using empirical discriminative analysis of rollout data, and show that their GTPO hybrid advantage formulation eliminates the advantage misalignment problem.

**Practical Results:**

On a representative task requiring flight cancellation under policy constraints and user manipulation, the base model generates 56 turns of verbose but ineffective reasoning. After training, the model completes the same task in 28 turns with 100% action accuracy in approximately 10 minutes.

## Dimension-Aware Reward Approaches

Diversity-aware Reward Adjustment (DRA) is a theoretically grounded framework that calibrates the reward signal using the semantic density of sampled groups, leveraging Submodular Mutual Information (SMI) to implement an Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS) mechanism that effectively de-biases the gradient estimation.

MMR-GRPO integrates Maximal Marginal Relevance to reweigh rewards based on completion diversity, with the key insight that semantically redundant completions contribute limited marginal learning signal; prioritizing diverse solutions yields more informative updates and accelerates convergence.

## Multi-Reward Handling

Recent research addresses challenges in multi-reward settings. GRPO suffers from reward signal collapse in multi-reward settings, where when different combinations of rollout rewards are normalized together, they collapse into identical advantage values, losing critical distinctions that guide learning. Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO) solves this by decoupling the normalization of individual rewards, more faithfully preserving their relative differences and enabling more accurate multi-reward optimization.

## 3D-Aware Reward Implementation

World-R1 uses a composite 3D reward that scores videos on three axes: meta-view plausibility (judged by Qwen3-VL), reconstruction fidelity (1 − LPIPS), and trajectory alignment — combined with an HPSv3 aesthetic reward to prevent quality collapse.

These approaches represent evolving methods to handle dimension-aware and multi-dimensional reward structures within GRPO-based training frameworks in 2026.

## GRPO Overview

GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), introduced in DeepSeekMath and operationalized at scale in DeepSeek-R1, has become the standard RL algorithm for LLM posttraining. It eliminates the value network by computing advantages within response groups — halving memory overhead vs. PPO — but has real failure modes (entropy collapse, advantage collapse, KL drift) that practitioners must actively manage.

## GRPO and Tool-Use Agents

The dominant posttraining recipe for capable tool-using agents in 2026 is a three-stage pipeline: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for format and cold-start, preference optimization (DPO/SimPO) for alignment, then reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (GRPO/DAPO) for reasoning and generalization.

## τ-Bench and τ²-Bench

τ-bench is a benchmark emulating dynamic conversations between a user (simulated by language models) and a language agent provided with domain-specific API tools and policy guidelines. The 2026 update (τ²-Bench) removed incorrect expected actions, clarified ambiguous instructions, fixed impossible constraints, and added missing fallback behaviors across airline, retail, and banking domains.
